after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 9 & 3\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =3\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 9 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3-3\text{i} & -2 \\ 9 & 3-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-3-3\text{i}){x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 9{x}_{1}+(3-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-3\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-3}{1-\text{i}}=\frac{-3(1+\text{i})}{2}=-\frac{3}{2}-\frac{3}{2}\text{i}.$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 13 & 1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1+3\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-1+3\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 13 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-1+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -1+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2-3\text{i} & -1 \\ 13 & 2-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-2-3\text{i}){x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ 13{x}_{1}+(2-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-1+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-2-3\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -(2+3\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2+3\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{-1}{2+3\text{i}}=\frac{-(2-3\text{i})}{13}=-\frac{2}{13}+\frac{3}{13}\text{i}.$

after.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-\sqrt{2}\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\sqrt{2}\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2+\sqrt{2}\text{i} & 2 \\ -3 & -2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+(-2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-\sqrt{2}\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{1}{2}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{-2}{2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}}=\frac{-2(2-\sqrt{2}\text{i})}{6}=-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{i}.$

EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=−2i, and

A−λI=[22−3−2]−[−2i00−2i]=[2+2i2−3−2+2i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(2+2i)x1+2x2=0−3x1+(−2+2i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−(−2i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

x2=−12(2+2i)x1

Therefore, the general solution is given by

[x1−12(2+2i)x1],x1∈C.

Setting x1=−2, we get the eigenvector

v=[−22+2i].

Finally, ab=−22+2i=−2(2−2i)6=−23+23i.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvector of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvalue
content.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-\sqrt{2}\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\sqrt{2}\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2+\sqrt{2}\text{i} & 2 \\ -3 & -2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+(-2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-\sqrt{2}\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{1}{2}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{-2}{2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}}=\frac{-2(2-\sqrt{2}\text{i})}{6}=-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{i}.$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ -5 & -3\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 5 \\ -5 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )-(-5)(5) & =0 \\ -15-5\lambda +3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(10)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{-36}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 6\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm 3\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =1\pm 3\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+3\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ -5 & -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4-3\text{i} & 5 \\ -5 & -4-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(4-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4+3\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=1-3\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4-3\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-5)(-5)}{(4+3\text{i})(4-3\text{i})}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix

\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 5 \\ -5 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )-(-5)(5) & =0 \\ -15-5\lambda +3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(10)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{-36}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 6\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm 3\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =1\pm 3\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+3\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ -5 & -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4-3\text{i} & 5 \\ -5 & -4-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(4-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4+3\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].

$$
